items.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
items.summary:
The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight

As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along.

The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation.
items.t: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses

items.title: Richard Russo’s Panic
items.summary:
1

Normally, my wife and I visit Martha’s Vineyard in September. It’s still summer then and the ocean remains warm, but the crowds have left. This year, though, we decided to spend a couple weeks on the island in June before the worst of those same crowds arrived. My new novel, Under the Falls , was publishing mid-summer, and it was unclear how long I’d be touring with it. It was possible we wouldn’t make it to the Vineyard until mid-September, if then. Also, visiting in June would make it easy for me to hop on the inter-island ferry and attend the Nantucket Book Festival and cross paths with some writer friends. The plan was for me to arrive there early in the morning of the festival’s first day, attend as many sessions as possible, then return to the Vineyard in the evening. Except no, that might not work. It would probably make more sense for me to stay the night and return the following morning. Barbara, my wife, had no desire to accompany me, for which I didn’t blame her. She’d toured with me the previous summer for Life and Art , my essay collection, and would hit the road with me later this summer for Under the Falls . I’ve been writing books and going on tour with them for four decades now, and Barbara, God love her, knows exactly what I’m going to say in my events’ Q&A sessions before I say it. Why not give her a well-deserved night off?

Still, when we went to bed that night, I was feeling more than a little anxious. In truth, my anxieties had been ramping up for some time. I’d actually diagnosed this as sanity. I mean, come on. A malignant narcissist president.…
items.t: Richard Russo’s Panic

items.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
items.summary:
A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence

In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud.

Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.

items.title: The History of the First Study on the Sex Lives of Women
items.summary:
Imagine yourself as a well-to-do white woman in 1921. In your experience, sex and reproduction are discussed in hushed tones, or not at all. Thus, you are surprised when you open the mailbox to find a letter from the Bureau of Social Hygiene in New York City.

Checking to be sure you are alone, you carefully open the envelope. “Dear Madam,” the letter begins. “Will you permit us to take the liberty of asking your intelligent and sympathetic cooperation in a very important sociological study?” The letter explains that the Bureau intends to make “wise education in matters of sex an integral part of the whole scheme of education.” You nod approvingly. But then you tighten your grip on the letter as you read on: “It is in directing the educational aspects of this movement that we need reliable information of the most personal nature…We have prepared a questionnaire for this purpose. The questions relate to the early sex information in girlhood, its sources and effects, and the sex experiences in girlhood, womanhood, and marriage.”

Surely this must be a mistake! Everyone knows that sex studies are conducted on “bad” women, on prostitutes or psychopaths. You, on the other hand, have always thought of yourself as a perfectly ordinary woman. You are normal ! What information could you possibly provide?

Unlike other sexuality studies, Davis’s book centered women’s experiences; unlike other works on women, it validated female sexuality.

Although you’re tempted to crumple up the letter and throw it in the dustbin, it is signed by the Bureau’s General Secretary, Dr. Katharine…
items.t: The History of the First Study on the Sex Lives of Women

items.title: Five Queer Holiday Romances to Read This Winter
items.summary:
If you say the words “sapphic holiday movie” to a group of queer women, I’d bet more than a couple of dollars that the conversation would quickly devolve into a debate about Hulu’s 2020 film Happiest Season .

Is it because everyone agrees it’s the pinnacle of queer holiday cinema? Or because many people online remain convinced that Kristen Stewart’s character should have ended up with Aubrey Plaza as a hot doctor?

No. It’s because, when it comes to mainstream queer holiday movies, the pickings are remarkably slim. There’s Carol . Let It Snow . Single All the Way . Meanwhile, straight people have everything from classics like Love Actually to a nearly bottomless supply of offbeat Hallmark movies.

This became painfully apparent to me in 2022, when my partner and I got COVID the week before Christmas. For our suddenly solo holiday celebration, we decided to watch every cheesy, cheery Christmas movie we could find. But we quickly discovered that there were so few holiday movies featuring queer characters (never mind centering them) that we got bored pretty fast.

I wanted more queer stories to enjoy during the holidays. And I couldn’t stop thinking about what their absence means during a season when so many LGBTQ+ people may need that joy the most.

That experience became part of the inspiration for my debut novel, A Very Merry Detour . Alaina sets off on a cross-country road trip determined to win back her ex-boyfriend, only to drive into a snowbank outside a tiny Utah town and into the orbit of Priscilla, its grumpy bookstore owner. As her feelings for Priscilla grow,…
items.t: Five Queer Holiday Romances to Read This Winter

items.title: The Strangeness of Expat Fiction: 100 Years of The Sun Also Rises
items.summary:
My students don’t like Hemingway. They abhor his misogyny. They reject the bulls, blood, and booze dirtying his pages. They can’t abide the Papa persona.

These students are hardly alone. Over the past forty years, Hemingway has fallen from academic grace. Apart from the contributors to The Hemingway Review , most scholars don’t publish articles or books on the writer. And, if they do teach his work, they usually limit themselves to In Our Time (1925) or The Sun Also Rises (1926). When it comes to literary studies, Hemingway no longer seems relevant.

On the face of it, the 100th anniversary of The Sun Also Rises  (1926) is unlikely to change this attitude or inspire lay readers to discover the Nobel Prize winner. With rare exception, students, professors, and literati could care less about the date. (Compare the minimal interest in Sun ’s anniversary with the hoopla surrounding the centenary of The Great Gatsby .) Yet I find this moment valuable: not to champion Papa, but to consider what the dominant critique of his work may have ignored. For all his limitations, Hemingway was unusually sensitive to the politics of national belonging and uncomfortably aware of changes in gender roles. His oeuvre played a more unorthodox role in US literary history than we’ve been willing to allow, and a reevaluation of The Sun Also Rises  brings his strangeness to the fore.

Jake’s troubled masculinity has everything to do with his sense of dislocation, with the difference life abroad inevitably entails.

This hypermacho text—cue the Pamplona bulls and the gallons of wine—worries about…

items.title: Kiran Desai on Writing In a Post-Colonial Context
items.summary:
The Center for Fiction welcomed award-winning author Kiran Desai for the launch of her luminous, Booker Prize-longlisted new novel, The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny . Marlon James , author of Black Leopard, Red Wolf and A Brief History of Seven Killings , joined Desai in conversation.

Exploring questions of class, history, and inheritance, Desai’s new novel is a sweeping, emotionally resonant meditation on identity, belonging, and the bonds that shape us.

From the conversation: 

Kiran Desai: I’m steeped in Jane Austen. Oh, it’s ridiculous, but Sherlock Holmes, Agatha Christie, all of that was childhood reading on the train, the plane.

Marlon James: Do you think those books still have some sort of influence on how you write?

KD: Probably. I mean, that was the English I grew up reading. I remember hearing you, Marlon, once saying that at one point you thought you were speaking or writing like the butler.

How do you think about migration, how do you push it out of there? How do you change the language?

MJ: Yeah. Damn. You’re really googling me. I was talking to some people, including people who may be in the audience,  about the type of English we grew up with.

Yeah. And, it wasn’t until I came to London I realized I sounded like the Butler because we learned this very sort of servile English. And actually, I can turn it into a question. How important is language to you and how your characters sound? The novel as well.

KD: It’s a real question about Indian English. Talking of Jane Austen, two things; the language and also growing up thinking that a novel is tied to…

items.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
items.summary:
Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

Continue reading...
items.t: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?

items.title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days
items.summary:
Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over

Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter.

The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do.

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Short Story Collections of 2026
items.summary:
It’s been a particularly fruitful year for the short story. In Recommended Reading alone, we’ve had the honor of publishing excerpts from many of our favorite collections of the year. Along with surprising variance and singularity, there are also recurrences across these collections: identity, artifice, and distance—both temporal and physical—mediate the relationships at the core of these books.

In her introduction to Lim Sunwoo’s story “That Unfamiliar Night,” translator Chi-Young Kim writes: “Lim beautifully portrays how grounding it can be when someone sees you, when someone is quietly there for you.” Across these collections, a reader has this sense of bearing witness—and being seen—by so many small moments. In Bret Anthony Johnston’s “Paradeability” , a father accompanies his son to a clown convention in Texas; the costumes and air of performance both amplify and conceal vulnerability. In Sydney Rende’s “Monsters” , the dissolution of a relationship is distorted in the funhouse mirror of reality TV. In “Going Up” from Chris Vanjonack’s Out of Body , an anonymous speaker targets a woman plagued by uncertainty. Above all, our favorite collections this year play with ambiguity: What can be revealed when a story withholds a tidy answer to its central questions? 

This year’s best works of short stories include five debut collections, as well as new collections from veterans of the form, such as Bret Anthony Johnston and Emily Ruskovich. Regardless of where you start, there are many delights to be found above—and below—the surface of these narratives.
–Lennie…

items.title: A Night at the 77th National Book Awards
items.summary:
The National Book Awards is arguably the year’s biggest night in books. It’s glam (Black-tie! Tuxedos! Champagne!), it’s fun (think cocktails on the dance floor next to literary all-stars), and, at its best, it’s political. It’s a moment for writers to take the stage and speak out against global injustice and the injustices we are facing from within our own industry. Last night’s ceremony was all of the above, and I got to experience it live, reporting the event with former Electric Lit intern Amulya Tadimety, who graciously helped me record the evening. (Shout out to Amulya, who even swapped phones with me so I could write down quotes while she took pictures using the higher-quality camera.)

This year featured a phenomenal set of finalists in all categories, many of whom Electric Lit is lucky to have featured in our digital pages. In Fiction, we featured an interview with Valeria Luiselli and a joint conversation with Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera , the two trans novelists nominated for the award—an exciting and much-deserved first that I hope marks many more to come. In Nonfiction, we published interviews with Abdelrahman ElGendy , Sara Nović , and Camonghne Felix , as well as a reading list from Joseph Osmundson , who also helped us put together an article about Bret Stephens’ hideous New York Times hit piece about the diversity of the year’s longlist.

items.title: What to Watch This Weekend, YA Edition
items.summary:
Netflix has been having a time with adaptations lately . There are so many great ones that are either birthed from YA novels or that reimagine stories with younger protagonists.

The following YA adaptations are available on Netflix . In them, love gets messy, one bullied teen in Brazil gets a summer he’ll never forget, and a sword-toting princess avenges her father.

To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before : It feels like this adaptation of the 2014 bestselling release by Jenny Han came at a time when the Netflix adaptation game wasn’t as strong. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if the success of this movie encouraged more YA adaptations. 

The 2018 release follows the book fairly closely, though there are also a few differences . High schooler Lara Jean’s world gets rocked when the love letters she wrote to her five crushes get mailed out to them. 

Here the Whole Time : This Brazilian-set coming-of-age film was adapted from a 2017 YA novel of the same name in English, but originally titled Quinze Dias by Vitor Martins, translated by Larissa Helena. 

Interestingly enough, the novel gets compared to To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before , except the main character is a fat gay teenager who finds out his crush is staying with him and his mother for 15 days one summer. 

Scarlet : This fantastical anime adaptation of Shakespeare’s Hamlet looks gorgeous. It follows a teen princess on a quest to avenge her father.
items.t: What to Watch This Weekend, YA Edition

items.title: A Call to Action from Electric Literature
items.summary:
Dear Reader,

Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was a blatant attack on trans people, period—and applying would have been a betrayal of the values held so closely by EL and its community. I was part of the decision to forgo funding, and while it was nerve-wracking to walk away from money we relied on, standing up for our beliefs was a no-brainer. We trusted that our community would have our back and fill the gap. And it did.

When I was preparing to take over as Executive Director and Publisher earlier this year, EL had the chance to speak publicly (in an amicus brief attached to a lawsuit targeting the NEA) about how the loss of NEA funding impacted our ability to practice free speech as an independent literary magazine. As I was interviewed by lawyers from the National Coalition Against Censorship, I took a moment to reflect on the prior year. I felt more sure of our decision than ever. Though our funding had been cut, though we had been forced to revise our financial strategy without notice, we stood with the communities whose rights, protection, and humanity we are forever committed to uplifting—trans people and the queer community, people of color, people with disability, immigrants, women. Rather than feeling fearful about what the future might hold, I only felt immense…

items.title: Literary Advocacy in the Wake of the Midterms: Book Censorship News, November 20, 2026
items.summary:
When it came to the candidates who will hold office and represent the people, the midterms were an overwhelming success for the freedom to read.

When it came to state- and local-level policies, referendums, and amendments, the midterms were much less successful.

With the results settling and the reality of 2027 just a little over a month away, literary advocates can continue their efforts to support anti-book ban, pro-public library, pro-public education. There’s a lot on the table across the country, and each step an individual takes builds the kind of momentum that helped ignite change, as we saw at the ballot box this month.

So where to begin?

Support Florida. Don’t Denigrate It or Write It Off. 

Florida did not “go blue” the way that Texas did, but races across the state were tremendously close. Several major democratic wins occurred in the very areas that republicans deliberately gerrymandered . Those republicans spent a lot of money on their candidates and their ballot measures, and the fact that several democrats came within just a few points of winning both showcases that Florida isn’t a “lost cause”. It highlights how deeply impacted voters are in the state by voter suppression, gerrymandering, and disenfranchisement. Rather than write off the state, it’s beyond high time for advocates to pay attention to and support those doing tremendous work on the ground to protect access to books, libraries, and public education.

items.title: The Horror of History: Historical Horror Novels
items.summary:
There’s a reason so much horror these days is set in the past: nothing is quite as creepy as the unfamiliar and unknown. For so much of human history, we’ve worked on hunches and guesswork to explain the world around us. Out of this guesswork grew the myths we all know and love today about vampires and werewolves and witches. But these creatures weren’t always viewed as myth. For much of history, they were believed to be very real. Even today, unexplained phenomena remain situated somewhere between science and magic, with paranormal explanations filling in the gaps until we can ascertain the truth of the things happening all around us.

Without artificial lighting, without medical knowledge, without near-instant mass communication, the known and unknown sat so much more closely side by side, which is exactly why history and horror go so well together in my mind. There’s nothing quite as atmospheric as a cliff-side gothic mansion, and there’s nothing quite as horrifying as a tale that defies all logic and reason. These historical horror novels, full of monsters both manmade and mythic, are proof of exactly that. Read them if you dare, and be thankful you at least can turn on a light to scare the shadows away.

items.title: How Ten National Book Award Finalists Tackle Writer’s Block
items.summary:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s  Craft of Writing  newsletter— sign up here . 

Some of this year’s National Book Award finalists and winners share their best advice for dealing with writer’s block, from writing by hand to reading widely.

*

Edwidge Danticat, author of Dèy 

I’ve never really had writer’s block, mostly because I refuse to acknowledge it. If something I’m writing and want to write isn’t coming, I simply tell myself it’s not ready yet, and I try to trust that it will arrive in its own time. During these times, I’ll read a lot or I’ll draft shorter pieces to keep my creative juices flowing. Middles are often where I get most stuck, after the excitement of a beginning fades, so I muddle through, writing very imperfect sentences and paragraphs until I find my way forward. I also try to use my down time from writing to reconnect with life beyond the page. Living more fully can sometimes bring the words back.

Morgan Thomas, author of Mad Eden 

Writer’s block takes different forms for me, and so responding requires discernment. Generally, if I’m not eager to write there’s a good reason. It signals that I need to tend other parts of my life — explore new books or music, spend time with my family, spend time with trees, go for a walk, rest. I try to listen. But I’ve also found that I’m always reluctant to work on stories or novels when they are about 75% done. The early glamour has worn away, but I’m not yet near enough to sense the ending’s presence. I’ve learned that I have to push through here, continuing in spite of my reluctance.

items.title: Why Fiction Loves Family Drama
items.summary:
There’s a house in my family—or, a house that used to be in my family. A beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that my stepfather’s stepbrother had inherited from a wealthy godmother. The place was laden with debt, and expensive to run, so he had to sell it—but that’s not the point. The point is that our family, like lots of families, is complicated, with enough steps to make a ladder. Which is perhaps why I’m drawn to reading, and writing, about other complicated families in fiction— see, we’re not the only ones .

Lucky for me, stories about dysfunctional parents, children, partners, ex-partners (the list goes on) are in good supply and always have been. The Greeks were all over family drama: in Euripides’ Medea , a mother murders her children to punish her faithless husband; there’s a bucketload of domestic bloodshed in Aeschylus’s Oresteia . The Old Testament is plagued with marital woes and sibling rivalries.

If Jane Austen were here today, she might tell us that we’re drawn to families under pressure because there’s no such thing as a family that isn’t under pressure; she might even say that it’s “a truth universally acknowledged” (etc). Which, together with her writing, witty and slyly funny, is surely the secret to the enduring appeal of her classic novels. Two hundred years on, they remain a hit at the box office, with new adaptations for every generation.

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026
items.summary:
This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we . In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them , these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest of us, trying to keep up?

Layli Long Soldier’s We (Wé) takes the question of we to its most elemental level. The Lakota word wé means blood, and Long Soldier uses it to explore family, nation, history, and language through poems, essays, and artwork. For Jake Skeets, we extends beyond people to the land and everything living on it. Horses opens with 200 feral horses stuck in Arizona mud and unfurls into an elegy for a changing Navajo Nation. Fatimah Asghar’s Daughter of the Mountains asks what remains after exile, reckoning with estranged kin and the landscape of their ancestors in poems both funny and elegiac. In Assembled Audience , the ever-delightful Erika Meitner takes up the strange business of being together, on beaches and in airports, in mourning and in protest. William Lessard’s haunting /face turns patents for facial capture technology into unlikely poetry about what happens when a face becomes data. And Hieu Minh Nguyen’s Staying Still traces the distance between the people and places we long to belong to and the selves we’re trying to become.

So much about who counts as us is now decided by people and machines that don’t know us at all. Against all that flattening, these poems get stubbornly specific. Maybe we begins there, not in agreement or allegiance, but in the…

items.title: In the Midst of Bingeing and Purging, My Job Theft Was A Silent Cry for Help
items.summary:
Stealing Space by Dayna Mahannah 

The gas station’s fluorescent lights glowed as I waited for the vehicles to clear their pumps. When the lot had emptied, I abandoned the till. I roamed the aisles, straightening candy products and rearranging the Hungry Man sub sandwiches in the fridge. The security camera had a blind spot where I could wedge myself, right up against the counter. I snuck a Danish, the syrupy glaze clinging to the wrapper like mucus. I chewed fast, facing the wall, and stuffed the packaging in the coffee station trash.

After pretending to organize the chocolate bar display in front of the till, I swiped a Mr. Big off the shelf, tucking it under the edge of my work shirt, and pushed open the side exit into the garage. Light beamed into the defunct repair shop. Dust motes glimmered, floating in the dark like phosphorescent plankton. Then the door shut, severing the shaft of light. Petroleum wafted up from the concrete floor. Standing on the stoop, my skin hot despite the frigid shop, I tore through the serrated edge of the candy wrapper, scarfing the chewy mess. I jammed the yellow wrapper underneath used oil containers in the recycling drum.

We experimented with tiny crimes like egging houses and stealing makeup from Zellers.

Back inside the station, a cursory check out the window showed no customers gassing up. I flipped the Back in 5 Minutes sign on the front door, turned the lock, raced for the bathroom, and drove my fingers down my esophagus until everything pushed out into the open.

I’d started working at the gas station in June, just as grade 10…

items.title: Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era
items.summary:
The Original Mother 

The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy . “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago. 

“A man.”

“Huh.”

“Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said.

Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!”

“Is that his name?”

Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?”

“The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?”

“Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack.

They lapsed into silence. 

The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear. 

“Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said. 

The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand. 

The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each…

items.title: Two Trans Novelists Have Broken the National Book Awards’ Glass Ceiling
items.summary:
Tonight the winners of the 77th National Book Awards will be announced. Though this will be published before we know which authors ultimately receive the grand honor, I already know that the finalists this year uniquely—and with exquisite, hard-earned artistic merit—speak to the ever-evolving state of American literature.

Two of the finalists for the National Book Award in Fiction are trans—only the second and third openly trans authors ever to be nominated in this category. At no fault of trans writers, and all fault of the societal powers that be: This simply was not possible even a decade ago. If we’re not careful, it might not be possible once again, even before the next presidential term. It’s for this reason, additional to the fact of their literary genius, that I consider myself greatly privileged to spotlight National Book Award finalists Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera.

From untangling the increasingly hostile and anti-trans US political landscape in Thomas’s Mad Eden , to exploring Colombia’s lively queer underground scene in Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , both of these authors’ novels prove to be unprecedented in craft, and unchallengeably excellent. Over Zoom, email, and voice notes, Thomas, Lopera, and I discussed the complexity of labels in trans and neurodivergent communities, the nuances of capturing queer joy, and the difficult onus of representation for minority authors.

Jalen Giovanni Jones: So first, I’d like to congratulate you both on the many accolades that these beautiful novels brought you, particularly you both being…
items.t: Two Trans Novelists Have Broken the National Book Awards’ Glass Ceiling
